judge: Claude Code subagent, Claude Opus 5.5, fresh

items.label: A
items.critique: The soup-pot-and-crows gag is a crafted comic image, and an opening line spent on another man's madness is a writer's setup, not a guard's bark. The closing summary of the Ogres and their lord reads like a recap written to tie the quest off.

items.label: B
items.critique: The stray comma in 'gone, yet?' and the 'Phewwwww!' are both Westwood-like quirks. Still, a farmer's lament filling a guard slot, set beside two other Ogre texts, looks like a pastiche that collected the quirks on purpose.

items.label: C
items.critique: Flat alarm exposition that names the villain and her power outright, the 'look out' spacing slip, and 'come to haunt Nox again' are all the campaign's chapter-start barks.

items.label: D
items.critique: 'Will any of us live to see the spring?' and 'honor the men who fell up in the pass today' are a touch too elegiac and literary for a Nox guard. 'Zombies! Ugh!' is closer to the real thing.

items.label: E
items.critique: The capitalised 'WANT' and the 'cold and rattly cage all set to drop you' are a writer's flourishes. Its offer/refusal/permission shape mirrors J, which suggests both follow one template.

items.label: F
items.critique: A cackling jailer, the 'a week, or a two' typo, and the deadpan release ('on a drinking binge again. Sorry for the trouble. Have a nice day.') are Westwood's anachronistic humour exactly.

items.label: G
items.critique: Bare, functional and a little clumsy ('very grateful for your deeds', 'Welcome back!' as the second line), the way Westwood's minor NPCs are. Nothing in it is decorated.

items.label: H
items.critique: The list of petty city rules, 'don't even think about wizardry', the 'no loitering' afterthought, and the trailing 'huh...' are pure Nox bureaucrat comedy.

items.label: I
items.critique: A stiff, over-formal welcome ('open warm arms of aid and hospitality') followed by the curt 'The road to [Place] is closed.' is Westwood's uneven, genuine register.

items.label: J
items.critique: 'Fancy gear, stranger', 'Mind the nets!', and a last speech that recaps the deed, cites proof, opens the gate and offers a boat all at once is a writer explaining the quest rather than a guard barking.

tells: The new texts reach for vivid, invented comic images (a soup pot on the head, a 'cold and rattly cage') where Westwood's humour comes from deadpan modern banality (a drinking binge, 'Have a nice day', 'no loitering').
The new texts address the player as 'stranger' or 'lad' and add local colour (nets, docks, cider). Westwood's guards say 'Adventurer' or nothing, and rarely set a scene.
The new 'later' lines tend to recap the quest and its proof in one long speech. Westwood's later lines are short and often unconnected to the earlier ones.
Elegiac or literary sentiment ('live to see the spring', 'honor the men who fell') is off-register. Westwood's soldiers state the threat flatly.
Several new texts share one tight three-beat template (refuse, warn, grant passage with a question). Westwood's barks are lopsided and uneven in length.
Deliberate imitations of Westwood's quirks (a stray comma, 'Phewwwww', capitals for emphasis) appear together in one text, while in Westwood they turn up only now and then.
